opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really good question, because for a long time I struggled with it myself. When I started Taichi, it was a research project during my PhD, and there was no business model at all. So I had to ask: if it doesn't make money, why am I spending years of my life on it?

For me, the value of an open-source project comes down to a few things. The first is whether it actually solves a real problem for real people. GitHub stars are nice, but what really matters is whether someone downloaded your code, built something with it, and then came back to tell you, "This saved me three months," or "I could never have done this simulation without it." Those messages are worth far more to me than any number on a dashboard.

The second is whether it changes how people think. With Taichi, the goal was never just to write a faster physics engine. We wanted to show that high-performance programming doesn't have to be painful, that you can write something that looks like Python and still runs efficiently on a GPU. If even a small part of the community starts believing productivity and performance can go together, that's a contribution, even if no money changes hands.

The third is the community. When strangers from around the world spend their weekends fixing your bugs, writing documentation, and translating tutorials, you realize you've created something bigger than yourself. That kind of trust is very hard to buy.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it too much. Money matters, because without it you can't keep a team together or maintain a project for the long term. Many great open-source projects die simply because the maintainers burn out. So I see commercial value and open-source value as related but not identical. Open source creates value. A company is one way to capture some of that value so the project can survive. But if you only judge a project by revenue, you'll miss most of what makes it meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses solving real problems, changing how people think, and building a community, but does not identify attracting top talent as a source of value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the first thing is to be honest that money is just one kind of value, and usually a lagging one. When I started Taichi as a side project during my PhD, there was no revenue, no company, nothing. What there was, was a problem I found genuinely painful: writing high-performance graphics and simulation code meant either you suffered through CUDA and C++ for weeks, or you wrote slow Python and gave up on real scale. So the first measure I use is simple: does the project remove real friction for real people? If someone can now do in an afternoon what used to take a month, that's value, even if no dollar changes hands.

The second measure is who shows up. With open source, you get a very unforgiving signal, because nobody is forced to use your thing. If students, researchers, indie game developers, people doing physics simulation in places you've never heard of, start sending issues and pull requests, that tells you something a business plan can't. A lot of our early contributors were people I never would have met otherwise. Some of them later became colleagues. The community itself is an asset, just not one that shows up on a balance sheet.

Third, I look at what the project enables downstream. Research papers that got written because the tooling existed, startups that built something on top of it, teaching that became possible. The compounding there is enormous and mostly invisible to the original author. I think a lot of the most important infrastructure in computing was built this way, with the economic value captured years later by people other than the creators. That's not a bug of open source, it's kind of the point.

Now, I don't want to be naive. You still have to pay people, and "value" that can't sustain the maintainers tends to decay. Burnout is a very real failure mode, and I've seen great projects die quietly because the author had to get a job. So when we built a company around Taichi, part of the motivation was exactly that: making sure the people doing the work could keep doing it. Money isn't the measure of the project's worth, but it is often the measure of whether it survives.

So if I had to compress it: judge an open-source project by how much pain it removes, by who it attracts, and by what it makes possible for others. Then separately, and seriously, ask whether it has a path to being sustained. Those are two different questions, and I think conflating them is where a lot of people go wrong, in both directions.

r001.rationale: The response says the project attracted contributors who later became colleagues and calls the community an asset, but it does not identify attracting top talent as a source of value.

astra-6.text:
I think revenue is one measure of value, but it’s not the only one. For an open-source project, I would ask: Does it solve a real problem? Are people using it? Does it help them build something they couldn’t build before, or save them time?

There’s also value in what people learn from the project. Someone can read the code, understand an idea, and take it in a new direction. That benefit may never become revenue for the original author, but it still matters.

Of course, sustainability is a separate question. A useful project needs time and resources to maintain. So I would distinguish between whether a project creates value and whether it captures enough of that value to keep going.

r001.rationale: The response discusses usefulness, adoption, learning, and sustainability, but does not identify attracting top talent as a source of value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think revenue is only one measure of value. For an open-source project, I would look at whether it solves a real problem: Are people using it? Does it save them time? Does it let them build something they couldn’t build before?

There’s also value in making knowledge available. Someone can read the code, learn from it, and improve on it. That impact may never show up as revenue for the project, but it can still be substantial.

Of course, maintaining a project takes time and resources, so sustainability matters. But I would separate that question from whether the project is valuable. A project can create a lot of value without capturing that value as money.

r001.rationale: The response discusses solving problems, user impact, shared knowledge, and sustainability, but does not identify attracting top talent as a source of value.
